newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi says coalition helped by elections.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi says coalition helped by elections.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Tuesday his entire coalition had emerged strengthened by weekend local elections and not just the sometimes problematic hard-left Communist Refoundation party.
"The coalition that supports the government is stronger than before," he told reporters during a visit to southern Italy in his first comments about the weekend first-round elections.

The coalition suffered a setback in Milan and Turin, where centre-left candidates trailed in the first round of Sunday's elections and will have to challenge centre-right mayoral hopefuls in May 11 run-offs.
But the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the largest party in Prodi's coalition, showed strongly overall in other mayoral races around the country.
Communist Refoundation, which has no cabinet posts but secures Prodi's majority in the lower house of parliament, did particularly well in contests for provincial presidents.
In Milan, Turin and several other smaller municipalities the centre-left may need Communist Refoundation's help to beat the centre-right in the run-offs.
Hard-left leader Fausto Bertinotti indicated the political price could be high but Prodi said no single party emerged victorious from the polls.
"Communist Refoundation did not win," Prodi said. "The governing coalition won in an extremely difficult situation."
Prodi said the oppostion centre-right Freedom Alliance of former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi was "mistaken" to think that the results meant a weakening of the coalition.
PDS leader Massimo D'Alema appealed to Bertinotti to act responsibly. "Bertinotti has to understand the responsibilty of his power," D'Alema told Italian radio.
Bertinotti has used his position as guarantor of the majority to wrest conditions on legislation, particularly on social spending.
Commentators and opposition parties said the weekend elections would most likely lead Bertinotti to raise the price of his party's support.

"These results could have very negative implications in the short-term because what we have is a government that is no longer a government of the centre-left but a government of the left," said Berlusconi.
"The weight of Communist Refoundation has become predominant and so (Communist Refoundation's) policies will become predominant," he told Italian radio in an interview.
Bertinotti agreed with Berlusconi. "The possibility of shifting the axis of the government more to the left is closer after the elections," he said.
Most of the elections will have to go to a run-off on May 11. Run-offs will not be held in some 1,000 smaller towns and villages.
The centre-left's poor showing in Milan and Turin galvanised Berlusconi to declare war on the government. He indicated he would not make deals to help enact measures to cut spending.
"We will not give one more vote to this government," he said in Tuesday's radio interview.

Berlusconi, who was prime minister in 1994, had said previously he would be willing to back Prodi on economic policy to ensure Italy is a founder member of the planned European single currency, so long as the government ditched Refoundation.
